debate_title: Do AI benchmark scores predict real-world usefulness?

conflicts.point: Whether mandatory pre-market certification standards or continuous live telemetry loops are the appropriate primary governance mechanism for high-consequence artificial intelligence deployments.

positions.stance: High-stakes institutional procurement requires mandatory pre-market certification and independent robustness audits to prevent irreversible operational catastrophes.
Mandatory pre-market certification creates bureaucratic delays that cause quantifiable human harm by withholding beneficial technology, making agile telemetry and rapid iteration preferable.

conflicts.point: Whether human-in-the-loop validation constitutes an engine of continuous algorithmic capabilities scaling or a labor subsidy masking underlying model brittleness.

positions.stance: Human correction loops directly update model weights and drive rapid capabilities scaling as a core technical feature.
Human correction loops function as an externalized repair shop that patches foundational model failures using low-wage precarious labor.

verdicts.conflict: Whether mandatory pre-market certification standards or continuous live telemetry loops are the appropriate primary governance mechanism for high-consequence artificial intelligence deployments.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist position names a specific enforcement institution, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, and a concrete mechanism of legally binding pre-deployment audits. The accelerationist counter-argument relies on abstract claims about zero-day shifts without detailing how to prevent catastrophic failures before deployment.

verdicts.conflict: Whether human-in-the-loop validation constitutes an engine of continuous algorithmic capabilities scaling or a labor subsidy masking underlying model brittleness.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic position cites documented evidence regarding vendor reliance on ghost workforces in the Global South to patch real-time production failures. The accelerationist stance offers a theoretical reframing without presenting concrete empirical proof that human correction loops directly drive algorithmic scaling rather than masking model errors.
